title: Why Train Tracks Sit on a Pile of Rocks
sources: TxDOT Rail Design Manual 'Ballast' / Wikipedia 'Track ballast' / Trains.com 'Track ballast' / Mental Floss 'Why are there crushed stones alongside railroad tracks?': crossties spread the load of the rails; ballast is crushed (angular) stone that interlocks to hold the ties in place, lets water drain away and keeps the track bed from turning to mud

Wikipedia 'Rail fastening system' (tie plates) / American-Rails.com 'Railroad spikes' / Trains.com 'What holds railroad track in place?': steel tie plates and spikes hold the rails to the ties and keep them at gauge; US standard gauge is 4 ft 8 1/2 in (Britannica 'Gauge', Wikipedia 'Standard-gauge railway')

FRA 'Track Buckling Prevention' training module / FRA 'Track Buckling Prevention: Theory, Safety Concepts and Applications' (2013): steel rails expand in heat; continuous welded rail can buckle sideways on hot days ('sun kink')

Practical Engineering 'Why Railroads Don't Need Expansion Joints' (2023) / RailwayNews 'Continuous Welded Rail explained': old jointed track had small gaps at bolted joints for expansion, which made the clickety-clack sound; welded rail removes them
Britannica 'Welded rail' / Union Pacific 'Long Rail Is a Game Changer' (2015) / Trains.com: rails are welded into long strings (typically 1,440 ft; UP long rail 1,600 ft), i.e. over a quarter mile

Wikipedia 'Rail stressing' / SafeRack glossary 'Rail neutral temperature' / SunRail CWR plan: welded rail is heated or stretched with hydraulic tensors before it is fastened, so it is stress-free at a warm 'neutral' temperature (about 90-110 F) and only buckles on very hot days

lines.text: If you lay steel rails straight on the dirt, the first heavy train pushes them into the ground.
lines.caps: If you lay steel rails | straight on the *dirt, | the first heavy train | pushes them | into the ground.

lines.text: So you lay wooden ties underneath, to spread the weight out wide.
lines.caps: So you lay wooden *ties | underneath, to spread | the weight out wide.

lines.text: But then it rains, the dirt turns to mud, and the ties start sinking too.
lines.caps: But then it rains, | the dirt turns to *mud, | and the ties start sinking too.

lines.text: So you dig it out, and pour in a thick bed of sharp, crushed rock, called ballast.
lines.caps: So you dig it out, | and pour in a thick bed | of sharp, crushed rock, | called *ballast.

lines.text: Water drains straight through it, and the sharp edges lock together, so the ties can't slide.
lines.caps: Water drains straight through it, | and the sharp edges | lock together, | so the ties can't slide.

lines.text: But every train shoves the rails sideways, and they slowly creep apart.
lines.caps: But every train shoves | the rails sideways, | and they slowly creep apart.

lines.text: So you nail them down with steel plates and spikes, exactly four feet, eight and a half inches apart.
lines.caps: So you nail them down | with steel plates and *spikes, | exactly | *4'8½" apart.

lines.text: But in the summer sun, steel grows, and the rail can bend sideways into a sun kink.
lines.caps: But in the summer sun, | steel grows, | and the rail can bend | sideways into a sun *kink.

lines.text: Old tracks left small gaps between the rails. That's the clickety-clack you hear.
lines.caps: Old tracks left | small gaps between the rails. | That's the *clickety-clack | you hear.

lines.text: Today, crews weld the rails into one long ribbon, over a quarter mile long.
lines.caps: Today, crews weld the rails | into one long *ribbon, | over a quarter mile long.

lines.text: And they stretch it tight before clamping it down, as if it were already a hot day.
lines.caps: And they stretch it tight | before clamping it down, | as if it were already | a hot day.

lines.text: Add a heavy train on top, and you've built a railroad track.
lines.caps: Add a heavy train on top, | and you've built | a *railroad track.
